analysis.one_liner: Caps gasoline prices during price-spikes, taxes oil windfall profits, blocks oil mergers, and raises fuel economy standards.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it sat in six House committees until the Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have let the President cap gasoline prices when anticompetitive conduct drives them up, required the government to release a million barrels a day from the emergency oil reserve until gas fell below $1.50 a gallon, taxed oil company profits above a 'reasonable' level at up to 100%, banned exporting Alaskan oil, and put a one-year freeze on large oil company mergers. It also raised fuel economy requirements for cars and light trucks after 2014 and gave tax credits to buyers of fuel-efficient vehicles built in the United States by union labor. It was referred to six committees the day it was introduced and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Motorists and households facing high gasoline prices, fuel-dependent businesses like trucking and farming, and buyers of efficient American-made vehicles if the bill had passed.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers and fuel-dependent households and businesses

how_it_helps.text: The President could cap wholesale and retail gasoline prices at or below their March 1, 2004 level when a significant price increase is substantially caused by conduct that lessens competition, with civil penalties up to $1 million per violation [S3].

The President would have to suspend deliveries to the Strategic Petroleum Reserve and release at least 1 million barrels of oil per day for up to 60 days, until the average gasoline price reported by the Energy Information Administration fell below $1.50 per gallon [S3].

An excise tax would apply to sales of crude oil, gasoline, and petroleum products, rising from 50% to 100% of profits above the 'reasonable profit' level set by an independent Reasonable Profits Board whose members may hold no financial interest in the businesses they judge [S3].

A one-year moratorium would bar mergers between large petroleum producers, refiners, distributors, and retailers, and future oil industry acquisitions would have to show a net benefit to consumers by maintaining or increasing competition [S3].
New passenger cars would have to average 45 miles per gallon and light trucks 34 mpg for model years after 2014, cutting what drivers pay at the pump over the life of a vehicle [S3].
Buyers of fuel-efficient passenger vehicles assembled in the United States under a collective bargaining agreement would get a tax credit of up to $6,000 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil producers, refiners, and marketers would bear the windfall tax, price caps, mandatory inventories, and merger freeze; automakers would bear the cost of meeting much higher fuel economy standards; buyers of large vehicles would face fewer options.

drawbacks.text: Price caps can cause shortages: when prices cannot rise, demand exceeds supply and rationing follows, a widely recognized risk from the 1970s price control experience that an honest supporter must weigh against the immediate relief to drivers.

The bill would draw down the emergency Strategic Petroleum Reserve by 1 million barrels a day and set a $1.50-per-gallon target far below then-current market prices, draining the nation's emergency stockpile and putting the government in the business of setting a fuel price target.

A windfall tax on profits above a board-determined 'reasonable' level could discourage oil investment and production, and the definition of reasonable profit would rest entirely with three presidential appointees.

The vehicle tax credit would apply only to vehicles assembled in the United States under a collective bargaining agreement, limiting choices for buyers and excluding most foreign-brand cars sold in America.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill attacked a real problem — 2005 saw gasoline prices spike past $3 a gallon after Hurricane Katrina, hitting household budgets and fuel-dependent businesses — and its fuel economy and antitrust provisions offered durable relief. But its most aggressive tools carried real design risks: price caps and a $1.50-per-gallon reserve drawdown could produce shortages or drain emergency supplies, and a tax on profits above an administratively set 'reasonable' level is hard to administer fairly. The efficiency standards and the windfall tax were the more conventional parts of the bill; the price-stabilization authority was the radical one.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to six committees on the day it was introduced; two subcommittees got the pieces, neither ever acted, and the bill died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter DeFazio introduced the bill with Rep. Bernard Sanders on July 28, 2005, and it drew 5 cosponsors (4 Democrats, 1 Independent) [S1][S4].
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and, in addition, to the Ways and Means, Government Reform, Judiciary, Resources, and International Relations Committees [S5].

In August 2005 it was referred to the Energy and Air Quality Subcommittee of Energy and Commerce and the Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee of Resources, and the record shows no hearings, markups, votes, or floor action afterward [S5].
The 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, so the bill never advanced beyond committee referral [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil producers and refiners avoided price caps, a windfall profits tax, and a merger freeze, and automakers kept the existing fuel economy standards; drivers kept paying market prices. The multi-committee referral structure meant no committee ever had to take a recorded position on it.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 5 cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent Sanders; the bill sat in committees of a Republican-controlled House that never acted on it, so the divide ran along party lines without ever reaching a vote.

industries.note: The bill would have capped their prices during anticompetitive spikes, taxed profits above a board-set 'reasonable' level at up to 100%, required minimum inventories, frozen large mergers for a year, and banned Alaskan oil exports. These measures existed to prevent the industry from profiting at the pump at consumers' expense.

The bill imposed much higher fuel economy standards (45 mpg cars, 34 mpg light trucks after 2014), a real compliance cost — but it paired that with a tax credit of up to $6,000 for efficient vehicles assembled in the U.S. under collective bargaining agreements, which favors unionized domestic plants. Drivers would save at the pump; the industry's interest in selling large, low-mileage vehicles ran against that.

The bill declared OPEC production cutbacks to be de facto price fixing and urged the President to file a World Trade Organization complaint, and it reimposed the ban on exporting Alaskan North Slope oil.
Lower gasoline prices through reserve releases and price stabilization would directly cut operating costs for businesses and farms that burn fuel; the bill's own findings name them as beneficiaries.
